topic: Two-level teaching architecture (Level 1 first principles, Level 2 institutional mechanics)
evidence_found: Chapter 1 teaches assets, liabilities, funds, mandates, benchmarks, risk, liquidity, horizons, basis points, fees, institutional investors and intermediaries in eight sections, each with Level 1 and Level 2 blocks, a worked example and self-test questions. The application has Beginner, Both and Technical views; caveat boxes sit outside Level 2 so the beginner view keeps them.
unresolved: Chapters written by different streams apply the two levels with slightly different density; chapters 6 to 8 use Level 2 less often than chapter 1.

topic: Seven questions for every important concept (what, why, who, what happens, how money moves, what can go wrong, why it matters to this role)
evidence_found: Applied explicitly in Chapter 1 to each core concept, including DB and DC pensions, LDI, money market funds and OCIO.
unresolved: Not applied as a fixed template in later chapters, where the concepts are behaviours and roles and a different structure fits better.

topic: Searchable glossary with every acronym defined at first use
evidence_found: About 190 glossary entries merged from three fragments (W1, W2, R2), each with a plain definition, mechanics and why it matters; searchable in the application and printed as Appendix K. Terms are linked from chapter text on first use per section.
unresolved: Four entries (CSG, CCG, TPW, AUS) in the W1 fragment defer to later chapters for the official wording; the PLSA rename is flagged unverified. Regulatory facts in Chapter 1 rest on nine sources, four of them snippet-only.

topic: Detailed comparison of sales and relationship management, with variation by firm and team
evidence_found: Chapter 6 compares objectives, daily activities, work products, client contact, knowledge, coordination, targets, negotiation, pressure and progression, and explains why 'sales wins, RM retains' is a first approximation. Goldman's own wording is verified: CSG labelled as sales; a Client Coverage Group defined as retaining and expanding existing relationships; a London team advert combining both.
unresolved: How the London desks actually divide sales and relationship management is not publicly established; the former intern's CSG/CCG split is an unverified account.

topic: Illustrative working days, sample work products and the client lifecycle
evidence_found: Five illustrative days (institutional sales, institutional RM, TPW sales, TPW RM, consultant relations), six fictional work products, 12 institutional lifecycle stages and 7 wealth-intermediary stages in data/lifecycle.json, and 13 role cards with decision rights in data/roles.json. All labelled illustrative or supported inference; no hours or task percentages are given.
unresolved: None of this is Goldman-specific; it is general industry practice.

topic: Misconceptions and the difficult parts of the work
evidence_found: Five misconceptions examined without replacement slogans; a section on repetition, uncertain cycles, rejection, internal dependencies, dissatisfied clients, fee pressure and explaining outcomes one did not control.

topic: Compensation evidence for sales versus relationship management
evidence_found: The £52k and £48k base-salary figures come only from the former intern. Research found one verified US example of a commission structure for a wealth-channel role and nothing public for London analysts.
unresolved: London analyst base pay and any sales/RM pay gap are not publicly established. No conclusion about role quality or prestige is drawn from them.

topic: Defining the relationship and identifying the real participants
evidence_found: Chapter 7 distinguishes five meanings of 'relationship' (rapport, professional confidence, contract, institutional continuity, decision value), maps the participants and their differing aims, and sets out what a relationship reveals that a factsheet cannot and the reverse. Verified examples of the cast: the parties named in the BAE Systems and Shell appointments.

topic: Trust explained through behaviour for eight components
evidence_found: Each of competence, reliability, honesty, responsiveness, confidentiality, willingness to challenge, transparency about limits and consistency has a definition, observable behaviour, an illustrative conversation, a trade-off, a client consequence and a commercial consequence. Includes the words used when you do not know, when a product is unsuitable, when performance disappoints and when a commitment cannot be met.
unresolved: Conversations are illustrative. One FCA Handbook rule could not be fetched and is marked supported inference; the academic trust model is cited from memory.

topic: Economics of relationships; when a relationship should end; branching long-term scenarios
evidence_found: Chapter 7 covers information asymmetry, repeated interaction, search and switching costs, incentives and governance with assumptions and limits; value created versus advantage from inertia; the conflict when the client's best outcome reduces the manager's fees; five-, ten- and twenty-year branching scenarios; individual versus institutional relationships; a translation table from abstract words to observable actions.
unresolved: Scenarios are constructed, not observed. No Goldman internal policy on any of this is public.

topic: Why-trees with challenges, objections, boundaries and counterfactuals
evidence_found: Nine trees and 76 nodes in data/why_trees.json (asset management, institutional clients, CSG, sales, relationship management, Goldman Sachs, long-term relationships, 'selling trust', 'I like understanding clients'), six to seven levels deep with a branch point each, five counterfactual tests per tree, a different-role signal and a stated terminus.
unresolved: Removed from the outputs at the user's request (15 November 2026). The source files are kept in archive/.

topic: Question bank with argument, 30-second and 60 to 90-second versions and harder follow-ups
evidence_found: 34 questions in 11 categories in data/interview.json. Each has an underlying argument with source markers, the evidence it depends on, a realistic weak answer with diagnosis, two timed versions and three or more follow-ups. The six challenges named in the brief appear verbatim.
unresolved: These are practice questions, not predictions. Goldman-specific points rest on verified claims as at 14 November 2026 and should be rechecked before use.

evidence_found: Six practice criteria (accuracy, specificity, logic, judgement, clarity, supported personal evidence) with descriptions of a 0 and a 3; confidence earns no points.
unresolved: Goldman Sachs's actual scoring criteria are not publicly established. The framework is this project's proposal and is labelled as such everywhere it appears.

evidence_found: Six fictional cases: performance disappointment, a fee challenge, an unsuitable allocation request, an unfamiliar technical question, an internal delay, and a client considering a cheaper alternative. Each sets realistic junior decision rights, what good looks like, traps, model reasoning and follow-ups.
unresolved: Fee rates and sizes in the cases are invented round numbers.

evidence_found: Answers are written in a provisional first person with marked slots for the user's own examples; Chapter 10 explains how to fill them and that 'not yet tested' is an acceptable answer.
unresolved: No slot is filled. Answers that depend on personal evidence are incomplete until the user supplies it.

topic: Audit of recruitment-process claims used in preparation
evidence_found: Verified from Goldman's careers site: a roughly 30-minute first-round video interview and a Superday of two to five interviews; nine to ten week programme; four-application limit.
unresolved: Not publicly established: team allocation from video answers, double-speed review, interviewer order, in-person format and AI questions. Chapter 10 advises against keyword tactics built on them.
